statements.quote: 1.Creativity Assessment Battery (CAB): A standardized instrument comprising three subtests - musical divergent thinking, compositional flexibility, creative originality- which has provided evidence of reliability (Cronbach's α=0.87) for measuring creativity within the context of music composition.
statements.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 2795), Sec. 3.2 Research Tools, instrument 1.

statements.quote: 2.Technology Acceptance and Measurement Scale (TAMS): A 15 item Likert scale questionnaire measuring students’ perception of usefulness and easiness of AI composition tools which was adapted from Davis’ original TAM model. Its construct validity was confirmed through factor analysis (CFI=0.94, RMSEA=0.056).
statements.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 2795), Sec. 3.2 Research Tools, instrument 2.

statements.quote: 3.Compositional Product Assessment Rubric (CPAR): A comprehensive assessment framework which captures nine dimensions of musical compositions, such as melodic originality, harmonic sophistication, structural coherence, cultural integration, and others. The rubric has been validated by a panel of five expert composers who established inter-rater reliability of 0.83.
statements.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 2795), Sec. 3.2 Research Tools, instrument 3.

statements.quote: 4.Semi-Structured Interview Protocol: This is a qualitative assessment instrument made up of 12 questions aimed at exploring students’ AI composition process, strategic and non-strategic creative decision-making processes, and their technology perceptions.
statements.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 2795), Sec. 3.2 Research Tools, instrument 4.

statements.quote: 5.AI-Assisted Composition Platform (AICP): A purpose-built educational technology platform that integrates generative artificial neural networks with composition assistance features tailored to the specialized needs of music pedagogy, set for beginner and intermediate music learners.
statements.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 2795), Sec. 3.2 Research Tools, instrument 5.

statements.quote: All tools went through pilot sessions for fine-tuning with a sample of 28 music students who were not part of the primary study, ensuring alignment with educational goals as well as cultural relevance.
statements.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 2795), Sec. 3.2 Research Tools, final paragraph.

statements.quote: This research employed a systematic approach to information provision in order to ensure all information collected was reliable and thorough. The primary source of information data was 120 music students from four institutions offering specialised music programmes in Guangdong Province. The collection processes complied with ethical standards for research involving human subjects; all subjects signed consent forms, and approval from the institutional review board was secured prior to commencing the research.
statements.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 2795), Sec. 3.3 Data Collection, first paragraph.

statements.quote: The subjects were provided with demographic and baseline questionnaires along with creativity self-assessments before the first tests, which measured composition skills and technological attitudes. During the 12-week intervention phase, both groups, experimental and control, were subjected to process tracking and observational data collection which was carried out collaboratively for all participants. The data collection after the intervention phase incorporated new qualitative measures such as interviews with stratified participants, while all prior measures were repeated.
statements.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 2795), Sec. 3.3 Data Collection, second paragraph.

statements.quote: Participant confidentiality, as well as data integrity, were enhanced with participant identity encryption and restricted programme access based on role. Quantitative data collection was executed in predetermined non-alterable forms flagged with access restrictions to guarantee confidentiality. The qualitative data obtained from interviews and observations were recorded on audio, then solely transcribed, and checked by research assistants for any changes before final editing. Participant demographics together with the study’s numerical metrics can be referenced in Table 1 in detail.
statements.locator: PDF p. 7 (printed p. 2796), Sec. 3.3 Data Collection, continuation before Table 1.

statements.quote: This study utilised the mixed-methods approach to analyse the effect AI-assisted composition tools have on students’ creative capabilities. Quantitative data was analysed using SPSS version 27.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY), with a significance level of set α = 0.05 for all statistical tests.
statements.locator: PDF p. 7 (printed p. 2796), Sec. 3.4 Data Analysis, first paragraph.

statements.quote: Thematic analysis techniques were conducted through NVivo 14 software for qualitative data obtained from interviews and open-ended responses. The analysis was done through a six-step process which included familiarisation, initial coding, development of themes, review, definition, and reporting. The data was coded by two independent researchers and disagreements, if any, resolved through consensus discussions. Member checking with some participants was done to validate the thematic framework.
statements.locator: PDF p. 8 (printed p. 2797), Sec. 3.4 Data Analysis, continuation.

statements.quote: The overarching curriculum design included five sequential modules, which were completed within the framework of the 12-week intervention period. Specific to each module are learning objectives, instructional activities, methods of assessment, and technological integration which align with the music composition education standards. All components in the experimental group are captured in the module design framework highlighted in Table 2.
statements.locator: PDF p. 8 (printed p. 2797), Sec. 4.1 Teaching Model for AI-Assisted Composition Tool Integration; refers to Table 2 on PDF p. 9.

statements.quote: The design team captured all logs of implementation, carried out several observational rounds, and systematically processed the data during the pedagogy’s design intervention window.
statements.locator: PDF p. 11 (printed p. 2800), Sec. 4.3 Implementation Process, first paragraph.

statements.quote: To provide detailed insight into specific compositions, Table 7 presents assessment scores for representative exemplary works from both groups.
statements.locator: PDF p. 18 (printed p. 2807), Sec. 5.3 Music Composition Quality Multi-Dimensional Assessment; refers to Table 7 on PDF p. 20.

statements.quote: Compositions were scored on a scale of 1-5 by a panel of five expert evaluators. EXP = Experimental Group (AI-assisted); CON = Control Group (Traditional).
In Figure 6, the entropy-weighted comprehensive scores for all 120 student compositions have been ranked from highest to lowest.
statements.locator: PDF p. 22 (printed p. 2811), Sec. 5.5, first sentence immediately below Figure 6.

searches.relevant: HTTP 200 at https://learning-gate.com/index.php/2576-8484/article/view/8493. Only one article PDF is listed; no supplementary dataset, code, materials or registry links. The displayed 'Download data is not yet available.' appears under usage metrics and is not a research-data availability statement. PDF viewer and both observed download URLs also returned HTTP 200. The downloaded 25-page PDF (831,319 bytes) is byte-identical to the saved source PDF.

notes:
No public data deposit attributable to c618 was found. The entire 81,379-character markdown conversion (631 lines) was read, including all references and closing declarations; the 25-page published PDF contains no appendix. PDF text was used to verify relevant methods, confidentiality, selected-score and closing-declaration passages. The screening form has one study, S1, and both data_and_code URLs are empty.

No explicit data/code/materials availability statement, on-request offer, preregistration, repository identifier, external appendix or supplementary-file reference is given. The statements below quote descriptions of study instruments, data handling, software, printed data/examples and closing declarations; none provides access to a research dataset. Quotes are taken from the source markdown without paraphrasing. The role-based access restrictions in Sec. 3.3 concern internal confidential data handling; they do not establish a restricted-access public deposit or an application route.

The article itself is not counted as a data deposit. Tables 5-6 provide group summaries. Table 7 (PDF p. 20, printed p. 2809) prints ten deliberately selected exemplary compositions, five per arm, with Composition ID, Group, nine dimension scores and Average Score. These are composition IDs, with no confirmed participant-to-composition mapping. They do not supply the full 120-person sample, individual pre/post records, per-rater scores, or the underlying music/texts/ideas. The full corpus cannot be reconstructed from those selected rows or the plotted rank distribution.

No public data were found to resolve final.open_items concerning participant/output aggregation and mapping [3], conflicting Figure 6 rank/threshold counts [4], entropy-weight/composite calculation [5], or unreported CAB/MANCOVA results [7]. The instrument descriptions do not supply the detailed CPAR anchors/rater instructions [6], and no protocol resolves assignment [0], test-time AI access [1] or timing [2]. Consequently what_we_could_compute is null: no new sample-wide participant means, SDs, SEs, analyzed counts or diversity measures can be confirmed from a public dataset.

Rejected author-name candidates are recorded in searches rather than deposits. For OSF jzy5r, its public page, node metadata, osfstorage file listing, children, contributors, contributor node list and the Hypotheses.docx download all returned HTTP 200. The API listed exactly one file (13,370 bytes) and zero child nodes; its in-memory text concerns actors/victims in online dating. The two ComposerX record APIs returned HTTP 200 and list 000075.pdf of 226 bytes (record 14877130) and 704,819 bytes (record 14877425), respectively; the record descriptions establish that they are unrelated work. Harvard's YiWang contents API returned HTTP 200 and lists only the unrelated spin-torque dataset. No study data file was identified for row/column inspection.

All network calls used Python urllib with User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1, without an email address, authentication or access requests. No web search or GitHub API calls were used. Only in-memory downloads were used. DataCite, Harvard and OSF search page sizes were 100; the broad 175-result DataCite search was paginated. Zenodo initially rejected size=100 with HTTP 400; its documented response allowed unauthenticated size=25, which succeeded. Failed searches retain null result counts. Repeated identical queries made to recover concise audit output are consolidated by query; both pages of a paginated query share one total.

Paper-link HTTP checks (reference links are not deposits for this study): https://doi.org/10.55214/25768484.v9i6.8493 -> HTTP 200 (https://learning-gate.com/index.php/2576-8484/article/view/8493); https://learning-gate.com/index.php/2576-8484/article/view/8493 -> HTTP 200; https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ -> HTTP 200; https://doi.org/10.3390/technologies11020042 -> HTTP 403 (https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7080/11/2/42); https://doi.org/10.1155/2022/7616619 -> HTTP 403 (https://www.hindawi.com/journals/misy/2022/7616619/); https://doi.org/10.2307/249008 -> HTTP 403 (https://misq.umn.edu/misq/article/13/3/319/191/Perceived-Usefulness-Perceived-Ease-of-Use-and); https://doi.org/10.1177/21582440221085259 -> HTTP 403 (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/21582440221085259); https://doi.org/10.1080/13546783.2025.2485059 -> HTTP 403 (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/13546783.2025.2485059); https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.612739 -> HTTP 200 (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2021.612739/full); https://doi.org/10.1080/14613808.2021.1881054 -> HTTP 403 (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/14613808.2021.1881054); https://orcid.org/0009-0002-8410-8360 -> HTTP 200. Confidence is medium for the negative availability finding: the source paper and publisher were fully accessible, and all four required search APIs ultimately worked, but a common author name and repository indexing limits leave the possibility of an unlinked or differently titled deposit. The article's CC BY license is not evidence that an undiscovered dataset is public or licensed.
